extracted.intended_audience: historians and general readers interested in Elizabethan exploration, colonization, and the Raleigh/Hariot voyages
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, expectations, and practices around Elizabethan patents and colonization ventures (e.g., Gilbert's and Raleigh's patents), plus what made voyage accounts and collections authoritative. Covers legal limits, obligations, publication and political strategy in late 16th-century English western planting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent territorial scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant for 'two hundred leagues of any American coast not occupied by a Christian prince.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents specified the territorial extent a grantee could claim; they applied only to coasts 'not occupied by a Christian prince' (i.e., unpossessed by other Christian states).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent duration and forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: This grant was limited to six years, to expire ... in case no settlement was made or colony founded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents carried explicit time limits (commonly six years) and would lapse if no settlement/colony was established within the term; founding a colony was the central condition to retain rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary confirmation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Raleigh's patent ... required the confirmation of Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royal grants intended for major enterprises often needed parliamentary confirmation to secure their legal standing and to fend off rival claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantee obligations: conquer, colonize, Christianize, explore and survey
rubrics_metrics.description: Philip gave him almost unlimited power over Florida, with directions to conquer, colonize, Christianize, explore and survey, and all these too at his own expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees were commonly charged with multiple active duties — military/control actions, settlement, missionary activity, and systematic exploration/surveying — and were expected to finance these efforts themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified objectives and geographic tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: He was to survey the coasts up to Chesapeake Bay, explore inlets and find out the hidden straits to Cathay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents often contained concrete geographic and exploratory mandates (specific coasts to survey, inlets to explore, even the search for passages), which provided measurable expectations of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture and rival patents due to negligence or non‑success
rubrics_metrics.description: This patent also, like Gilbert's, in case of negligence or non-success, was limited to six years. ... five of Gilbert's six years having already expired without his obtaining success or possession, several others ... began agitation for rival patents in 1583.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to meet patent conditions invited forfeiture and created openings for competing claimants to seek rival patents — a patent-holder therefore faced political as well as practical pressure to act promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective possession requires settlement and towns, not mere paper claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Spain however still claimed possession, on paper, of the whole coast up to Newfoundland, though she could not boast of a single place of actual occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diplomatic/legal claims without founding towns or continuous occupation were weak; establishing settlements (towns, missions) was the recognized means to convert 'paper' claims into effective possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of published discourses and patronage to secure political and commercial support
rubrics_metrics.description: Hakluyt's Discourse ... was intended probably to prime the ministry and the Parliament, to enable Raleigh first to secure the confirmation of his patent, and afterwards the co-operation and active interest of the nobility and gentry in his enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing learned/polemical works, circulating reports, and cultivating influential patrons (ministers, nobility, merchants) were standard tactics to win parliamentary confirmation, raise funds, and enlist collaborators for colonial ventures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for authenticity of voyage accounts and collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Harlot's text and map with White's drawings are necessary complements to each other ... Thus the famous Collections of De Bry may be said to be of English origin, for to Raleigh and his magi De Bry owed everything in the start of his great work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary collections/narratives were deemed authentic and authoritative when they were based on primary reports, surveys/maps, and original drawings made by participants (e.g., Hariot's report + White's drawings + Hakluyt's editorial role); provenance and endorsement by known figures (Raleigh, Hakluyt) bolstered credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication strategy for voyage narratives (illustration and multilingual editions)
rubrics_metrics.description: De Bry ... engraved, printed, and issued his VIRGINIA in four languages, English, French, Latin and German ... The first was illustrated from the portfolio of John White, and the second from that of Jaques Le Moyne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful dissemination of voyage accounts combined high‑quality illustrations (maps, drawings) and wide linguistic reach (multilingual editions) to maximize impact, authority, and reuse across European audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational requirement: supply and reinforcement expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: They had long been expecting supplies and reinforcements from home, which not arriving, on the departure of Drake's fleet becoming dejected and homesick, they petitioned the Governor for permission to return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colonies depended on timely resupply and reinforcement; failures in supply could doom settlements regardless of initial establishment, so logistical planning was an implicit criterion for colonial viability.
